p: Paul describes a man living with his father's wife, probably his stepmother, a union the Law and Roman law both forbade.
b: Paul says "his father's wife," not "his mother," so most readers take her to be the man's stepmother. The Law forbids it and calls it uncovering the father's nakedness (Leviticus 18:8; Leviticus 20:11; Deuteronomy 22:30; Deuteronomy 27:20). Paul says even the Gentiles do not do this, and Roman law agrees: the jurist Gaius lists a stepmother among the women a man may not marry (Institutes 1.63). The Greek says the man "has" her, which can mean marriage or living together. Whether the father was dead or divorced, or still alive, is not said, and Paul does not name the woman, perhaps because she was not a believer. Nothing is said about her being disciplined.

p: The Greek porneia covers prostitution and, by Paul's day, sexual relations the Law forbids.
b: Porneia comes from pornē, "prostitute," and in Paul's world it could name any sexual act outside lawful marriage. Here it names a forbidden union of the kind listed in Leviticus 18. The site renders the word "sexual sin" everywhere (as in Acts 15:29 and Matthew 19:9), so a reader can follow it from verse to verse here (5:9, 5:11; 6:9, 13, 18; 7:2). The English "fornication" (KJV) is narrower than the Greek, and "immorality" is wider than the sexual meaning.

p: A word Paul uses six times in this letter for the pride that the Corinthians mistake for spiritual maturity.
b: Phusioō means to swell up or inflate, like a bellows. Paul uses it of the Corinthians' pride in their teachers (4:6, 18-19), here of their pride in a case that should shame them, and of "knowledge" (8:1); in 13:4 love "is not puffed up." Some commentators think the Corinthians were proud of the man's freedom, or of their own tolerance, as a sign of spiritual freedom; others think they were simply proud of themselves in spite of the case. Paul wants mourning, the response to a death in the family, not boasting.

p: Paul writes as if present in spirit and has already judged; he asks the church to act, and does not act alone.
b: Paul is in Ephesus (16:8) and judges the case "in spirit" as though present. His verdict is already made, yet the action is the church's: they are to gather (5:4) and act. Commentators differ on how much power Paul claims. Some stress his apostolic authority, which carries "the power of our Lord Jesus." Others stress that the whole community meets and shares in the act, as Matthew 18:15-18 expects. Both are in the text, and the churches have built their different pictures of church discipline on whichever they emphasize (see the card).

a: hand such a man over to Satan
p: Paul's order is hard to read: expulsion, bodily suffering, or both, with the man's rescue as the aim.
b: The picture is a man put out of the church into Satan's sphere (the world outside), where Satan has power over his "flesh." Readings differ. (1) Expulsion alone: "flesh" is his sinful nature, which is to be destroyed by the shock of being cut off. (2) Illness or death: "flesh" is the body, as in Job 2:6, where Satan is given power over Job's body. Some commentators allow a bodily meaning, and 11:30 links sin and sickness in this church. (3) A mix of the two. All agree that the aim is rescue: "that his spirit may be saved." Paul uses the same phrase of Hymenaeus and Alexander in 1 Timothy 1:20, "that they may learn not to blaspheme." Some also link this man with the one in 2 Corinthians 2:5-11, though many commentators doubt it.

a: on the day of the Lord
p: The Old Testament's day of the LORD is, for Paul, the day of the Lord Jesus.
b: In the prophets "the day of the LORD" is the day when God acts to judge and to rescue (Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31). Paul gives the phrase to Jesus: "the day of the Lord" here, "the day of our Lord Jesus" in 1:8. The oldest text of 5:5 has only "Lord" (see the variant); the Byzantine text adds "Jesus." The idea matters for the case: the man's spirit is to be saved on that last day, when judgment of the whole church is also coming (3:13; 4:5).

p: In the Bible yeast usually stands for something small that spreads, and here for the spread of sin.
b: Yeast in the ancient world was a lump of old fermenting dough kept from the last batch, so it carried the old batch into the new. Jesus warns of the yeast of the Pharisees (Mark 8:15), and Paul uses the same proverb in Galatians 5:9. In the Passover rule, leavened bread was cleared from the house because it stood for what went before (Exodus 12:15). Paul's point is that one unjudged case spreads through the church. This is not a hard line against sinners: in 5:9-13 he says exactly whom this applies to.

p: Paul calls Christ the slaughtered Passover and tells the church to live as the unleavened bread of that feast.
b: Exodus says, "you will get rid of the leaven in your houses" (Exodus 12:15), and Jewish households still search the house for leaven on the eve of the fourteenth of Nisan (Mishnah Pesahim 1:1). Paul uses this: because our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered, the church must clear out its old yeast. The Greek says only "our Passover" (to pascha hēmōn), meaning the Passover animal; the Plain keeps "Passover" and does not add "lamb" (the verb etuthē is "was slaughtered," a word used of sacrificial killing). The command ("Sweep out") and the statement ("you are already unleavened") sit side by side: be what you are. John's Gospel also links Jesus' death to the Passover lamb (John 19:36 with Exodus 12:46). Paul says in 16:8 that he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, which may mean he wrote in the spring, but the season is not certain. If the letter was read near Passover, a Gentile church was hearing a Jewish feast given a new meaning.

p: Paul may mean the whole Christian life, or a literal Passover and Unleavened Bread kept by the church.
b: Is Paul thinking of an actual feast, or of the whole Christian life as one long festival? Chrysostom and many others take it as the whole life of the believer, The Roman rite offers 1 Corinthians 5:6-8 as an optional second reading on Easter Sunday. Others think that this Gentile church, led by Paul, may have kept Passover with a new meaning, and they note that Acts has Paul marking Passover days (Acts 20:6). The Greek is a present command: "let us keep celebrating." What matters for the case is the contrast: sincerity and truth take the place of malice and evil.

p: Paul refers to an earlier letter to Corinth that we do not have.
b: This is not our 1 Corinthians. Paul had already written to say "do not mix with people who commit sexual sin," and the Corinthians had taken it too widely or twisted it, so Paul now corrects the misreading (5:10). Other letters between Paul and Corinth are known from the text: the Corinthians' own letter (7:1) and the "tearful letter" of 2 Corinthians 2:3-4 and 7:8. Some scholars think part of the earlier letter survives in 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1, which talks about mixing with unbelievers; this is a proposal, and many scholars reject it.

t: What does not eating together mean?
p: Paul bans table fellowship with a believer who lives in open sin; the churches disagree on what meal he means.
b: Meals were the center of ancient social life, and sharing a table meant acceptance. The ban probably covers ordinary meals and the church's common meal that held the Lord's Supper (11:17-34). Some think it means only the Lord's Supper, others any shared meal. Paul's list names six kinds of persons: the sexual sinner, the greedy, the idol worshiper (which could be a business contact), the slanderer, the drunkard and the swindler. Five of the six are not exotic; they are people a church would meet in daily life. The rule applies to a person "called a brother," not to unbelievers (5:10), and the church's later practice of shunning (see the card) is drawn partly from this line.

p: Paul takes the Torah's formula for cleansing the community and applies it to the church.
b: The words come from a refrain in Deuteronomy, in the Greek Old Testament: "you will remove the evil from among you." The site's Plain of Deuteronomy 17:7 reads, "So you will sweep the evil out from among you." The Hebrew verb means to burn out or sweep away. Deuteronomy uses the refrain for capital crimes (Deuteronomy 13:5; Deuteronomy 17:7; Deuteronomy 19:19; Deuteronomy 21:21; Deuteronomy 22:21, 22, 24; Deuteronomy 24:7). The offense of 5:1 is named in other verses: Deuteronomy 27:20 is a curse on the man who lies with his father's wife, and Deuteronomy 22:30 forbids it, but neither carries the refrain. Paul borrows the penalty formula and changes the penalty from death to removal. "The evil person" can also be heard as "the evil one" (Satan; Matthew 13:19), but the Deuteronomy background points to a person.
r: Deuteronomy 13:5; Deuteronomy 17:7; Deuteronomy 19:19; Deuteronomy 21:21; Deuteronomy 22:21; Deuteronomy 22:24; Deuteronomy 24:7

p: Roman courts favored the rich, and a lawsuit between believers brought the church's quarrel before pagan judges.
b: In a Roman colony such as Corinth, civil suits were heard by a magistrate or by a panel of jurors drawn from the wealthy. Judges and juries were often friends or clients of the powerful, so a rich plaintiff had the advantage over a poor defendant. Some scholars think the Corinthian cases came from the church's wealthier members, who could expect to do well in such courts. Paul calls the judges "the unrighteous," the same word he uses in 6:9. Jews had a long habit of settling disputes before their own elders. A saying recorded in the Talmud forbids using Gentile courts (Gittin 88b).

a: the saints will judge the world
p: Paul assumes the church knows the promise that God's people will share in judging.
b: The belief that God's people share in the final judgment goes back to Daniel 7, where "the judgment went to the holy ones of the Most High" (Daniel 7:22). Wisdom of Solomon 3:8 says the righteous will judge nations and rule over peoples. Jesus tells the Twelve they will sit on twelve thrones (Matthew 19:28), and Revelation 20:4 shows thrones given to those who judge. Paul says "Do you not know" six times in this chapter. He treats the idea as common knowledge from his first teaching in Corinth. Interpreters differ over whether the saints judge by taking part in Christ's verdict (a shared ruling) or by their lives standing as a witness against the world.
r: Daniel 7:22; Wisdom of Solomon 3:8; Matthew 19:28; Revelation 20:4; Luke 22:30

p: Paul does not say which angels or how; he uses the idea as an argument from the greater to the lesser.
b: The Greek says only "angels" and does not say which. Most take it to mean the rebel angels who are bound for judgment (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4), a belief also found in 1 Enoch. Others take it broadly as the angelic powers over the world. The sentence is an argument, not a lesson on the end times: if believers will judge such beings, they can settle a dispute over property. The Greek word for "everyday matters" (biōtika) comes from bios, ordinary life, and was used for business matters.

a: count for nothing in the church
p: The Greek can be a question or a command, and the 'despised ones' can be pagan judges or the church's least members.
b: The word means "despised, counted as nothing." Readings: (1) A question, with irony: do you set as judges the very people the church counts as nothing, meaning pagan judges (many commentators). (2) A command: "Set up as judges even those of no standing in the church," meaning its humblest members, who would still be wiser than the pagan magistrates. The Plain gives the question, which is how most editions punctuate it, and the tone fits 6:5, "I say this to make you ashamed."

p: Paul's advice to take the loss recalls Jesus' teaching to give up a coat as well as a cloak.
b: Why do you not "put up with the wrong"? The same ideal appears in Jesus' sayings about not resisting an evildoer and giving more to the one who sues (Matthew 5:39-40; Luke 6:29). Paul does not quote these sayings, and elsewhere he uses a saying of Jesus only when he says so (7:10; 9:14; 11:23). Some see a quiet echo here. Others see an ordinary Jewish and Greek wisdom that a loss is better than a feud. Paul's own point is that for the church the quarrel itself, not the property, is the defeat.

p: Malakos means soft; said of men, it is read as the passive partner in sex or as a man of unmanly luxury.
b: Malakos means "soft," like fine cloth (Matthew 11:8). When used of a man in moral writing it meant unmanly, indulgent or weak. Interpreters take it three ways. (1) The passive partner in sex between men, often a younger man or a slave Robert Gagnon holds this. (2) Male prostitutes. (3) A man of luxury and loose living, whatever his sexual partners. The KJV's "effeminate" follows (3). The Plain keeps the plain Greek meaning and leaves the reader to weigh the readings.

p: A word that appears first in Paul; its two halves, 'male' and 'bed', echo the Greek of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13.
b: Arsenokoitēs is a compound of arsēn, "male," and koitē, "bed." No example is certain before 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10. The Greek Old Testament of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 has meta arsenos koitēn, "with a male, a bed," and many scholars (Richard Hays among them) think Paul coined the word from that text. The site's Plain of Leviticus 18:22 has "With a male do not lie down in the ways of lying down with a woman." Others, such as Dale Martin, argue that the word names exploitation, such as male prostitution or the use of boys, since later writers use it with economic or abusive senses. The Plain gives the literal sense. Which acts it covers is the debated question. See the card, and Romans 1:26-27 for Paul's other text.

a: will not inherit the kingdom of God
p: Paul lists ten kinds of wrongdoing, then tells the Corinthians that they were once like this.
b: The list resembles other lists in Paul's letters (Romans 1:29-31; Galatians 5:19-21; Ephesians 5:5) and in Greek moral writers, and it mixes sexual sins (sexual sin, adultery, soft men, men who lie with males) with sins of property (thieves, the greedy, swindlers) and of speech and drink (slanderers, drunkards). "Inherit" is a promise word: the kingdom is a family inheritance from God (Matthew 25:34; Galatians 4:30). The point is not that one slip bars anyone, but that a life ruled by these things is not the life of the kingdom, and the church lives under the kingdom already. Paul's next line (6:11) describes the change that has already happened.

p: Three verbs describe one event of becoming a believer; the first is probably baptism.
b: The three Greek verbs are in the past tense, and the first is in the middle voice, so it may mean "you washed yourselves" or "you had yourselves washed." Most take it to be baptism (Acts 22:16: "have yourself baptized, and have your sins washed away"; Titus 3:5). The churches do not agree on what baptism does (see Acts and Romans 6 for those cards). "Made holy" and "justified" are not later steps after "washed." They are three pictures of one change. The sequence is also a Trinitarian one: in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God. The Plain's "justified" uses the site's usual term for dikaioō. Catholic and Orthodox teachers read the verb as "made righteous," a real change in the person, where the Plain keeps the site's standing rendering "justified."

p: Paul seems to be quoting a motto of some Corinthians and answering it.
b: Many scholars believe that 6:12-20 quotes slogans from the Corinthian church: "Everything is permitted for me" (6:12); "Foods are for the stomach" (6:13); and perhaps "Every sin ... lies outside the body" (6:18). Paul accepts the first in part and corrects it twice: not everything helps, and he will not be mastered by anything. Jerome Murphy-O'Connor wrote on the slogans of these verses in 1978, and many modern translations mark them with quotation marks. Others say there is no proof and that Paul himself is speaking in his own voice. Where the Plain uses quotation marks (6:12, 6:13, 7:1, 8:1, 8:4, 8:10), it follows the view that Paul is quoting; the Greek has no marks, and every one is an editorial decision of the Plain. The same slogan appears in 10:23, where the Plain also renders it "permitted." The pun is lost in English: the Greek words exestin, "it is permitted," and exousiasthēsomai, "I will be brought under authority," are related words.

a: Foods are for the stomach, and the stomach is for foods.
p: The slogan says that bodily desires are natural and passing; Paul says the body is not like the stomach.
b: The motto reasons from food to sex: both are bodily appetites that God made, and both are passing. Paul agrees that God will bring an end to the stomach and to foods, but he denies the second step. The body (sōma) is a different thing: it is "for the Lord," and it will be raised (6:14; 15:44). This is one of Paul's clearest statements that the body is not an empty vessel. Greek philosophy often treated the body as a container for the soul, to be dropped. Paul's view of the body is closer to the Jewish idea of the whole person.

p: The proof that the body matters is that God raised Jesus' body and will raise ours.
b: The sentence moves from the Lord's resurrection to ours, as chapter 15 will do at length (15:12-23). Paul's argument here is practical: what God will raise cannot now be given to a prostitute. Some in Corinth denied a future bodily resurrection (15:12), perhaps because they held that the body was of no account, and this may be why they treated sex as indifferent. The Greek verb is future: God "will raise" us.

p: A strong refusal that Paul uses in his letters when an objection leads somewhere he cannot accept.
b: Mē genoito is literally "may it not happen." Paul uses it about fifteen times, mostly in Romans, and only here in the Corinthian letters (the site reads it 'By no means!' in Romans 6:2, 15). It marks the diatribe style of a teacher who answers an imagined opponent with an emphatic denial. The KJV's "God forbid" adds a word that is not in Greek.
orig: μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito), 'may it not be'

p: Corinth's name was a byword for sex in the Greek world, though its temple prostitution is doubted for Paul's day.
b: Greek writers used "Corinthian girl" for a prostitute (Plato, Republic 404d), and Strabo says the temple of Aphrodite in the old city owned more than a thousand temple slaves, courtesans dedicated to the goddess (Geography 8.6.20). The Roman city Paul knew was refounded in 44 BC, and many scholars doubt that this temple prostitution continued then. Paul does not mention a temple: he speaks of a plain prostitute, and in the ancient city the banquets that the "knowledgeable" attended (8:10) often ended with prostitutes hired for the evening. The Greek for "parts" is melē, the limbs of a body, as in 12:12-27.

a: The two will become one flesh
p: Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 to show that even sex with a prostitute makes a bond.
b: The Plain of Genesis 2:24 is: "So a man leaves his father and his mother and sticks close to his wife, and they become one flesh." Paul's Greek follows the Septuagint, which adds "the two." The Masoretic Hebrew text does not have the word, but the Samaritan Pentateuch and other ancient versions do (Jesus quotes it the same way, Matthew 19:5). He uses the verb "joins himself" (kollaomai), a relative of the verb for "sticks close" in the Greek of Genesis (proskollaomai), and moves from "wife" to "prostitute." A bond is made even where there is no covenant, and that is the point. The one who is "joined to the Lord" (6:17) also becomes one with him: not one flesh, but one spirit.

a: Every sin that anyone does lies outside the body.
p: Either a Corinthian slogan that Paul corrects, or Paul's own comparison with other sins.
b: The line is odd, because Paul himself knows that sins such as drunkenness (6:10) harm the body. Two readings: (1) it is the slogan of some Corinthians ("all other sins are outside the body," so the body is not affected by sex), and Paul answers with "but the person who sins sexually sins against his own body." (2) Paul is speaking and makes a comparison: sexual sin touches the body in a way other sins do not (Calvin). The result is the same: sexual sin joins the body to something it was not made for. "His own body" may point to marriage, where husband and wife belong to each other (7:4). The Plain leaves the first clause without quotation marks. Whether it is a slogan is not certain, and the marks used elsewhere in the Plain are editorial decisions (see the note on 6:12).

a: a temple of the Holy Spirit
p: Paul pictures the believer's body as the place where God's Spirit lives, as the Jerusalem temple was God's house.
b: In 3:16-17 Paul says "you" (plural) are God's temple, meaning the church. Here "your body" is singular but the "you" is plural, so the Greek can be read as "your bodies, as a group" or as each person's body. Commentators have taken it both ways. The Greek word is naos, the inner shrine where the god was thought to live, not the whole temple area (hieron). The Plain says "temple" here, as in 3:16-17, 2 Corinthians 6:16 and Ephesians 2:21, even though it says "sanctuary" for naos in Matthew, Mark, Luke and Acts. In Paul the word is a picture, believers as the place where God lives, and "temple" is the natural English for that picture. Pagan Corinthians knew temples as houses of gods. Paul's picture is that the Spirit lives in the person and the person is God's, so a body given to a prostitute is a shrine misused.

a: you were bought, and a price was paid
p: The picture is a slave sale; Paul says Christ's death was the price, and Christians now belong to him.
b: In the ancient world a slave was "bought." Paul uses the picture again in 7:23, and Jesus gives his life as a ransom (Mark 10:45; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 1:18). The sentence does not say to whom the price was paid, and later theology has argued about it (see Romans 3 for the cards on the atonement). Adolf Deissmann once suggested that Paul had in mind sacral manumission, in which a slave "sold" to a god (as at Delphi) became free in law; others doubt that this is the source. The point is clear without it: the Corinthians do not own their bodies.

p: 'Not to touch a woman' means not to have sex; some think the Corinthians wrote this, and Paul answers.
b: Paul begins to answer the church's letter (the words "Now about" mark each topic: 7:1, 7:25; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1). The line "It is good for a man not to touch a woman" is either (1) a Corinthian slogan from their letter, which Paul qualifies (7:2-7), or (2) Paul's own opinion, which he then balances. The old KJV leaves it unquoted; the Plain follows the first view with quotation marks. This is the most disputed use of them in the Plain, and the variants list gives the reading with no marks. "Touch" is a Greek and Hebrew euphemism for sex (Genesis 20:6 uses the word of Abimelech and Sarah). The idea that the spiritual should leave sex behind might come from Corinthians who thought they already lived in the new age (4:8; 15:12), as some think, or from Greek ideas of the body. Paul agrees that singleness is good (7:7-8) but refuses to make it a rule.

p: Ancient Jewish law already gave a wife a right to sex; Paul gives it to both partners equally.
b: The Greek word is "the debt." In the Law a husband must not cut back a wife's "rights as a wife" (Exodus 21:10), and the Mishnah later set how often a husband must meet this duty, depending on his work (Ketubot 5:6). The surprise here is the "likewise": the wife has the same claim on her husband. In a Roman world where the husband held the power in the house, Paul's equal pairs (7:3, 4, 12-16) were unusual. Some manuscripts add "goodwill," which the KJV has as "due benevolence" (see the variant).

a: no authority over her own body
p: Paul gives the husband and the wife the same authority over each other's body, which was unusual for his time.
b: The verb exousiazō means to have authority over. It is the same root as the verb in 6:12, "I will not come under the authority of anything." In the Corinthian household the husband was legally the head, so a wife's authority over her husband's body goes against custom. Paul does not use the language of the husband's headship here (he does in 11:3; see the note there). Many readers take this as Paul's strongest statement that marriage is a partnership of rights, whatever else they conclude about roles.

p: A couple who stops sex without agreement, or for too long, may be tempted.
b: "Test" and "tempt" are one Greek word (peirazō). Satan is also the tester in 5:5, where the man is handed over to him. Paul allows a short time of abstaining for prayer if both agree. The same idea is in the Testament of Naphtali 8:8 (in the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, a Jewish work that many scholars think Christian hands later revised), which says there is a time for intercourse and a time to abstain for prayer, and in Exodus 19:15, where the people were told before the meeting at Sinai, "Do not come near a woman." Some later manuscripts add fasting (see the variant).

p: 'This' may mean the short break in 7:5, or the whole permission to marry in 7:2-5.
b: Sungnōmē is a "concession" or "permission" given by someone who understands human weakness. What does "this" point to? The break for prayer in 7:5 (most), marriage as a whole (7:2-5), or the advice to resume marital life after a break. Augustine took the concession to cover intercourse for self-control rather than for children, and thought it a small fault (The Good of Marriage); Luther and others replied that marriage is God's good order, not a mere concession. The Plain keeps the neutral "allow." The word is the opposite of a command (epitagē), which Paul uses in 7:25.

a: a gift of his own from God
p: Paul calls both singleness and marriage a gift; the churches disagree on whether celibacy is a higher calling.
b: "Gift" is charisma, from charis, "grace" (see 12:4 for the gifts of the Spirit). Paul does not rank them, but he does say he wishes everyone were as he is. His own situation is not clear: never married, widowed, or left by a wife are all proposed. Jesus speaks of eunuchs for the kingdom, "Let anyone who can make room for this make room for it" (Matthew 19:12). Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that the single life given to God is a high calling, and the Council of Trent teaches that it is better than marriage. Luther and Calvin taught that few have this gift and that most should marry. See the card.

t: Better to marry than to burn
p: 'Burn' is most often taken as burning with desire, but other readings have been held.
b: The Greek verb is puroomai, "to be set on fire." Nearly all take it as burning with sexual desire (as in the older Latin and Greek commentaries). Some have asked whether "burn" means punishment, as fire does in 3:15, but the talk of desire and self-control in 7:2 and 7:5 points to passion. Augustine used marriage as a remedy for lust, an idea that shaped Western views (The Good of Marriage); Orthodox teaching today stresses marriage as a path to holiness in itself. The reader should notice that Paul puts it as advice to people who lack self-control, not as the reason for marriage itself.

a: it is not mine but the Lord's
t: Paul and Jesus' teaching on divorce
p: Paul is citing a saying of Jesus, which the Gospels preserve in more than one form.
b: Paul says the Lord himself gave this order. Jesus' teaching on divorce appears in Mark 10:11-12 ("Anyone who divorces his wife and marries someone else commits adultery against her"), Luke 16:18 and Matthew 5:32 and 19:9, where Matthew adds the phrase "except for sexual sin." Paul's teaching is the earliest written version. He applies it to a Greek-speaking city where a wife could divorce her husband in Roman law, as Mark 10:12 also says. Paul gives no exception, and he does not say anything about the Matthew exception; whether he knew it is uncertain. Compare 7:12, where Paul says "I and not the Lord," and 7:25.

a: must not separate from her husband
t: Divorce in Jewish and Roman law
p: Jewish law let only a husband divorce; Roman law let either side end a marriage by notice.
b: In the Torah only the husband writes the certificate: "He writes her a certificate of divorce, puts it in her hand, and sends her away from his house" (Deuteronomy 24:1). In the first century the schools disagreed on grounds: Shammai allowed only some serious indecency, Hillel almost any reason (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). Roman law let either spouse end a marriage by informal notice, and Roman wives often did. Paul uses "separate" (chōrizō) of the wife and aphiēmi, literally "send away," of the husband. The Plain says "divorce" for aphiēmi in 7:11, 7:12 and 7:13, since Paul uses it of both husband and wife in 7:12-13. The two words are not likely to mean different things in law. The passage is about believers who think that being "spiritual" lets them leave a marriage.

p: Paul allows separation but not a new marriage; the churches differ on whether other grounds free a person to remarry.
b: For a wife who does separate, Paul says she must stay "unmarried" or be reconciled. That excludes a new marriage while the first husband is alive (compare 7:39). The Catholic Church teaches that a valid marriage lasts until death and allows separation without remarriage (Catechism 1649). Other churches add grounds: adultery, desertion by an unbeliever (7:15), and sometimes abuse. The Eastern churches allow remarriage with penance. The Matthew exception clause is the root of most of this (Matthew 19:9). See the card at 7:10-16.

p: Paul separates what Jesus said from his own judgment, yet claims the authority of the Spirit.
b: Jesus left no teaching on marriage between a believer and an unbeliever (they were rare in his day), so Paul gives his own judgment. He does not say it is less binding: "this is what I order in all the churches" (7:17), and he thinks he has "God's Spirit" (7:40). Some see a saying of Jesus on one question and none on the other. The churches that appear on this site all receive Paul's letters as Scripture (for Catholic teaching see Dei Verbum 11), so this verse is not a line between them on that point; where they differ is how apostolic teaching is handed on and weighed, a larger question than this verse. The distinction shows that Paul knew a body of Jesus' sayings and handled it carefully.

p: Ezra's community sent away foreign wives; Paul tells believers not to divorce an unbelieving spouse.
b: Ezra's community made a covenant to send away foreign wives (Ezra 10:3). Nehemiah dealt with the same problem by rebuking the men and making them swear not to intermarry (Nehemiah 13:23-27), and Malachi attacks marrying "the daughter of a foreign god" (Malachi 2:11). Paul's Corinthian Gentile believers were in a different situation: a Gentile joined the church while the partner did not. His rule is not to divorce. A believer who stays with an unbelieving partner does not make the household unclean: holiness works the other way (7:14).

p: The unbelieving partner is 'made holy' in the believer, though not saved by it.
b: "Holy" (hagios) usually means set apart for God. Paul does not say the unbelieving husband is saved: 7:16 treats that as a hope. Readings: (1) holiness spreads from the believer to the marriage and children, so the home belongs to God; (2) the marriage is lawful, not a union of sin, so there is no need to leave it (an old and common view); (3) the unbeliever is brought under the church's influence and the hope of salvation. The idea is the opposite of Jewish purity law, where uncleanness spreads, as in Haggai 2:11-13. Here holiness spreads. The line about the children appears in the next note.

p: Paul calls the children of a mixed marriage 'holy'; the churches use this verse in the debate over infant baptism.
b: In Jewish terms "unclean" and "holy" are opposite states. Paul says the children of a home with one believer are "holy," not unclean. Churches that baptize infants cite this verse as a sign that children of believers belong to God's people (Calvin argued this in his commentary on 7:14). Baptist churches note that nothing here speaks of baptism and that the unbelieving spouse is called "holy" too, with no one thinking that makes them members. Scholars have argued over what the verse shows about the early church's practice. See the card. A Jewish reader may notice that no rule here depends on the mother's descent, a rule the rabbis fixed later.

a: not enslaved in cases like this
p: If an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer is 'not enslaved'; do they then remarry? The churches differ.
b: The Greek "has not been enslaved" (dedoulōtai) means that the believer is not tied to the marriage. Does it free him or her to marry again? The Reformed and Lutheran churches say yes, under the heading of "desertion" (Westminster Confession 24.6). Catholic law, in the "Pauline privilege," says that a non-sacramental marriage can be dissolved in favor of the faith after the other partner leaves (Code of Canon Law, canons 1143-1147). The older view in many churches is that the verse says only that the believer need not run after the departing partner. The Orthodox allow remarriage in some cases by church economy. See the card.

a: whether you will save your husband
p: 'How do you know?' can be hopeful (you may save him) or discouraging (you may not).
b: The question can be read two ways. (1) As a ground for staying: you might save your spouse, so do not leave (held by many ancient and modern commentators). (2) As a ground for letting go: you cannot know that you will save the other, so do not sacrifice peace for an uncertain result (held by some modern commentators). The Greek is the same. The verse fits well after "God has called us to live in peace" and sets a limit on how long to wait. Paul says "save" (sōzō) of the believer's witness, which is the human part, because in 1 Peter 3:1 the same hope is held out to wives of unbelievers.

p: Paul says this is his ruling in all the churches; it is practical advice that sets one pattern of calling.
b: The "rule" is that each person should live in the situation he or she was in when called: married or single, circumcised or not, slave or free. The rule is not absolute, because Paul adds exceptions (7:15, 7:21). Commentators call it a principle of "calling" (klēsis). "Walk" (peripateō) is the Hebrew idea of walking as a way of life.

a: He should not try to undo it.
p: Some Jews in the Greek world tried to hide their circumcision; Paul says not to.
b: The Greek verb means "to pull over," and refers to a minor operation, called epispasm, by which Jewish men tried to cover the marks of circumcision. It was done by Hellenizing Jews in gymnasiums, where men exercised naked. 1 Maccabees 1:15 says that in the days of Antiochus "They made foreskins for themselves," and Josephus tells of Jews who hid it (Antiquities 12.241). Paul tells a Jew who is now a believer not to undo it, and a Gentile not to be circumcised. The pattern matches his argument in Galatians 5:2-6.

p: Paul says circumcision is nothing and keeping God's commands counts; scholars debate which commands he means.
b: The sentence sounds odd: circumcision is itself a command (Genesis 17:10). Paul says it is "nothing," yet "keeping God's commands" matters. Galatians has parallels: "In Christ Jesus, circumcision has no strength and neither does uncircumcision. Only faith has strength, faith working through love" (Galatians 5:6), and "A new creation is what matters" (Galatians 6:15). Readings: (1) the moral commands, such as those summed up in love (Romans 13:8-10), with circumcision now outside them (a common view); (2) the commands of Christ (Galatians 6:2); (3) in the "Paul within Judaism" reading, Paul expects Jews who believe to keep the Torah, while Gentiles are not to take on circumcision; his rule here is about identity, not abolishing the law. Both Jewish and Gentile believers keep God's commands, but they are different commands.

a: Were you a slave when you were called?
p: Paul speaks to slaves as full members of the church, not only to their owners.
b: A large share of the people in a Roman city were slaves, and a church there would include them: domestic slaves, slaves who managed businesses, and freed slaves. Paul addresses them directly, which was unusual in an ancient letter. A slave in Roman law could be freed by the owner's will, by a formal act or an informal one, and often after years of service. Many saved money (peculium) to buy their freedom. A freed slave still owed duties to the former owner, who became a patron. Paul gives no ruling on slavery as an institution here, and a slave's baptism did not change legal status. The Plain keeps "slave," as the site does for doulos. See the topic page on slavery.

p: The Greek has no object after 'use': it can mean 'use your freedom' or 'use your slavery.'
b: The last words are literally "rather use," with no object stated. English has to supply one, and the Plain supplies "it" (the opportunity of freedom), following reading (1). (1) "Use the opportunity" of freedom: if you can be freed, take it. This is the reading of most modern translations and many older commentators. (2) "Use your slavery," that is, stay a slave even if you could be free; some scholars argue for it. The Greek starts with "but if indeed" (all' ei kai), which can mean "even if," favoring (2), or "if also," favoring (1). The surrounding verses say "remain" in the situation of calling, but 7:23 ("do not become slaves of people") leans toward freedom.

p: A freed slave still belonged to a patron; Paul says believers are the Lord's freed people and also Christ's slaves.
b: The Greek is apeleutheros, a freed slave, who in Rome stayed bound to the former owner by duties of respect and service. Paul says that the believing slave is the Lord's freed person, free of every other master, and the believing free person is Christ's slave. Some scholars note that "slave of Christ" was also a high title, since slaves of great households ran them. But Paul's pair does not make slavery harmless: the slave is freed by the Lord, and the free is bound. See Philemon 16 for how Paul speaks of a slave who has become a brother.

a: Do not become slaves of other people.
p: Paul says believers belong to Christ, so they should not give themselves to any human master.
b: What does it mean not to "become slaves of people"? (1) Literally: do not sell yourself into slavery to pay a debt or to get a job, which people in the empire did. (2) Figuratively: do not be ruled by human opinion, such as the party leaders of chapters 1-4. (3) The wider rule: Christ's price makes the believer his, and no human owner is to take his place. The words repeat 6:20, "you were bought." Gregory of Nyssa's fourth homily on Ecclesiastes (fourth century) condemns slaveholding sharply, though scholars disagree on whether it calls for ending slavery.

p: The 'virgins' are mainly unmarried young women, but the Greek word can include men.
b: Parthenos means a virgin, almost always a young unmarried woman. Revelation 14:4 uses it of men. The question from Corinth is about the unmarried: a daughter, a fiancée, a widow's young charge. Paul's "no command from the Lord" means that Jesus left no word on the question (compare 7:10, 12), and the apostle gives a judgment he thinks may be trusted. He can speak as "someone who has received mercy" because of his call (compare 15:9-10).

a: the pressure of the present time
p: Paul does not say what the pressure is: a famine, a coming persecution, or the end of the age.
b: The Greek anankē means pressure, necessity, constraint. "Present" can also mean "impending." Views: (1) a food shortage in Corinth; Tacitus reports poor harvests and famine at Rome, with grain for only about fifteen days, in the year of Claudius's fifth consulship (Annals 12.43), and some scholars link the pressure to grain shortages at Corinth; (2) the "birth pains" of the last days before Christ's return (Mark 13:8); (3) the ordinary hardships of life (7:28). Paul would be writing within a few years of a shortage if (1) is right. The Plain keeps the wide word "pressure." Whatever it was, Paul gives it as the reason for his advice, not as a rule for all times.

a: the time has been cut short
p: Paul pictures time as a sail drawn in, with little room left before the end.
b: The word sunestalmenos means "drawn together," used of furling a sail or shrinking something. Paul believes the age is ending (10:11 speaks of the end of the ages). He does not give a date, and in 15:51 he allows that some will still be alive when Christ returns. "From now on" the Christian lives as in a short time. His five "as if not" lines (7:29-31) are not a call to leave the world, because he has just told married people to stay married. They describe how to hold everything lightly.

a: the shape of this world is passing away
p: 'Shape' (schēma) is the outward form; Paul says the present arrangement of the world is on its way out.
b: The Greek schēma means the outward form, the way things look and are arranged, and was used of a costume or a posture. Paul does not say that the world (kosmos) itself is ending but that its present form is. The word "passing away" is a present verb: it is in motion. The picture is of the old age giving way to the new one that has begun in Christ (compare 2 Corinthians 5:17; Romans 12:2). This is the basis for Paul's "as if not" way of living. It keeps the Christian from clinging to the things of the world, but it does not end marriage, mourning, joy, buying or using.

p: The Greek word merimna covers both healthy care and unhealthy worry; Paul plays on both.
b: Merimna means care or worry and is used in the Gospels for the worry Jesus forbids (Matthew 6:25-34). Paul uses it three ways in a row: "free of cares" (amerimnos), the unmarried man "is concerned" with the things of the Lord, the married man "is concerned" with the things of the world. The Plain keeps the same English root. Paul does not treat concern for a spouse as a sin: it is needed. His point is that undivided attention to the Lord is easier without a family, not that married people serve less. The next verses balance both.

p: Paul says he is not setting a snare for them, as a hunter would.
b: The word brochos is a noose or snare, used for catching animals. Paul uses it to say that his advice is not a trap and not a binding rule. The point is that his advice is "for your own good," and the aim is "devotion to the Lord without distraction." The same distinction between command and advice is in 7:6, 7:25 and 7:40.

p: Verses 36-38 are among the hardest in the letter: is the man a father, a fiancé, or a partner in a 'spiritual marriage'?
b: The Greek says only "his virgin." Four readings: (1) Father and daughter: the man must decide whether to give his daughter in marriage; this is the usual sense of the verb in 7:38 and the older reading (the KJV). (2) Fiancé and fiancée: the man is engaged and wonders if he is wrong to delay; common among modern commentators, and it takes the verb as "marry." (3) "Spiritual marriage": a couple living together as celibates, a view some have held. (4) Guardian and ward: a man responsible for a young woman in his household. The Plain keeps "his virgin" in 7:36-37 and uses a wide phrase in 7:38, but its "past the bloom of youth" in 7:36 leans toward the father reading (see the next note).

a: she is past the bloom of youth
t: Hyperakmos: whose passion, or whose age?
p: The word can mean 'past her prime' (the woman) or 'strong in passion' (the man); the choice shapes the whole passage.
b: Hyperakmos is a rare word built from akmē, the peak or prime, plus "beyond" or "over." It can mean "past the peak," past the usual age for marriage, said of the woman. It can also mean "over the peak," with passions at their height, said of the man. The ESV and NIV take it the man's way, which suits the fiancé reading. The Plain takes it as the woman's age, which suits the father reading and differs from those translations. Both senses can be found in Greek, and the grammar of "if she is" (the verb is singular and has no stated subject) does not decide the matter.

a: the one who sees to the marriage of his virgin
p: The verb gamizō usually means 'give in marriage'; later Greek also uses it for 'marry'. The Plain's wording leaves both open.
b: The Greek verb gamizō is used in Jesus' sayings for people "given in marriage" (Matthew 22:30; Luke 20:35), which is its usual sense and favors the father reading. Later Greek also uses it for "marry," which favors the fiancé reading. The Plain renders the pair "sees to the marriage of ... does not see to it" so that neither reading is chosen. The later Greek text has a stronger compound, ekgamizō, "give in marriage," with no "his virgin" (see the variant), which makes the father reading easier. Either way Paul's verdict is the same: the one "does well," and the other "will do better." Neither is a ruling on whether engaged couples may marry, which Paul does permit in 7:36 and 7:28.

p: A widow may remarry, but 'only in the Lord,' usually taken to mean a fellow believer.
b: The phrase is short and has two main readings. (1) The new husband must be a Christian. This is the usual view. (2) The marriage must be made in the Christian way, with the Lord's will in view. In either case Paul sets aside the idea that a widow must stay single. The same phrase in 7:40 expresses Paul's wish that she stay as she is. Some early Christian writers took a harder line on a second marriage: Athenagoras (about AD 177) called it a "specious adultery" (Plea 33, in the New Advent translation), and Tertullian urged his wife not to remarry (To His Wife). Paul does not. In 1 Timothy 5:14 younger widows are advised to marry.

t: 'I think I also have the Spirit'
p: Paul says he thinks he has God's Spirit, which can be modest, ironic, or a claim of authority.
b: "I think" (dokō) can mean "I believe" or "it seems to me." Paul may be answering some who claim the Spirit's guidance for their strict views (the "spiritual" ones), and he says that he has the Spirit too. The statement is both modest and firm. All the churches that appear on this site receive Paul's letters as Scripture, so the verse is not a dividing line between them. Paul does not say he has a command of the Lord (7:25), only the Spirit's guidance. Either way, the chapter ends by returning to a question of authority.

p: In Corinth meat often came from temple sacrifices, so a meal could carry a religious meaning.
b: The Greek eidōlothuta means "things sacrificed to idols." In a Greek or Roman city, part of an animal was burned for the god, part went to the priests, and part was eaten by the worshiper or sold in the meat market. Temples also had dining rooms where families and clubs held feasts: excavators have found such rooms at Corinth, at the sanctuary of Asklepios and at the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore, and invitations on papyrus from Egypt ask a friend to dine "at the table of the lord Serapis" (Oxyrhynchus papyri 110, in the Serapeum, and 523, in a private house, both of the second century, as listed by Blue). Jews and Jewish believers avoided such meat, and the Jerusalem decree (Acts 15:29) kept the ban for Gentile believers. Revelation 2:14 and 2:20 treat eating idol food as a serious charge. Some read Paul as giving a different answer in chapters 8-10; others (Cheung, Gooch) argue that Paul still treats knowing participation in idol feasts as a religious problem.

p: 'We all have knowledge' is probably what some Corinthians wrote, and Paul qualifies it.
b: Paul begins with a quotation from the church's letter (see "Now about" in 7:1): "We all have knowledge." The knowledge in question is about idols and the one God (8:4). Paul agrees with the content (8:4-6) but not with how it is used. "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up" is his own answer. The "all" is also challenged: in 8:7 "not everyone has this knowledge." Some Corinthians (probably the better educated, who could afford to dine at banquets) took their freedom from idols as a mark of spiritual advance (see 4:6-10; 6:12).

p: 'Build up' is Paul's measure for every use of freedom and every gift in this letter.
b: The verb oikodomeō means to build, as of a house or a temple, and Paul uses it for strengthening a person or a church (10:23; 14:3-5, 12, 26). Here it is set against "puffs up," which is air. Knowledge that serves the self swells; love builds someone else. Notice that 8:10 uses the same verb with an ironic edge: the weak person's conscience will be "built up" (strengthened, in the wrong direction) to eat food sacrificed to idols. Chapter 13 develops what love is.

p: Paul turns the claim to knowledge around: what counts is being known by God.
b: The pattern recurs in Paul: in Galatians 4:9 he corrects "to know God" to "to be known by God," and in 13:12 he looks ahead to knowing fully as he is fully known. In the Old Testament, "to know" can mean to choose and care for (Amos 3:2; Jeremiah 1:5). To be known by God means to be loved by him first. Notice that the person who loves God is the one known by him; knowledge of God follows love rather than the reverse. The reading of the verse varies in the manuscripts (see the variant).

a: an idol is nothing in the world
t: An idol is nothing, and yet
p: Paul agrees that an idol has no power as a god, but in chapter 10 he warns that demons are at work behind idol worship.
b: The Old Testament mocks idols as empty: the Plain of Psalm 96:5 has "Every god of the peoples is a nothing-god," and Isaiah 41:24 says, "Look, you come from nothing, and your work from nothingness." Paul agrees that the idol is nothing as a god. But Deuteronomy 32:17 says, "They offered sacrifices to demons, not to God," and Paul quotes it in 10:20. So the "nothing" is not the whole story: nothing divine, yet not empty of spiritual forces. The tension is one reason Paul does not simply say "eat anything." Chapter 10 explains where he draws the line (see 10:14-22). The Plain puts quotation marks on both clauses of 8:4 ("an idol is nothing in the world" and "there is no God but one") because many scholars take them as two Corinthian slogans, like "all of us have knowledge" in 8:1. This is an editorial decision of the Plain; others hear Paul speaking in his own voice.

a: there is no God but one
p: Paul's phrase rests on the Jewish confession that the LORD is one.
b: This is the heart of Israel's faith. The Plain of Deuteronomy 6:4 is, "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one." Isaiah 45:5 says, "I am the LORD, and there is no one else; apart from me there is no God." A Jewish reader hears the Shema here, and also hears the gap between "one God" and the claim that idols are "nothing": Jewish teachers of the time were also unsure whether pagan gods were nothing or were spirits of some kind (Deuteronomy 32:17). Paul's confession of one God is the starting point on which Jews and Christians stand together, and in 8:6 he restates it in a way that has divided them.

p: The city had temples to many gods, and Caesar was also called 'lord' and 'son of god'.
b: Corinth had shrines to Aphrodite, Apollo, Asklepios, Demeter and Kore, Poseidon, and Isis and Serapis, and the worship of the emperors, which scholars date at Corinth from the first century. "Lord" (kyrios) was used of gods such as Serapis and, in time, of the emperor. When Paul says there are "many gods and many lords" he describes what his readers see in the street. The phrase "so-called gods" means things people call gods; it does not say the gods exist, and Paul's view of their reality is given in 10:20. The language sets up 8:6, where "God" and "Lord" are given to the Father and Jesus.

a: there is one God, the Father
p: Paul splits the Shema's words 'God' and 'Lord' between the Father and Jesus, so Jesus is in the confession.
b: The Greek of Deuteronomy 6:4 says "the Lord our God, the Lord is one." Paul says "one God, the Father ... one Lord, Jesus Christ," giving "God" to the Father and "Lord" to Jesus, and adds the statement that "all things" come from the one and through the other. Wright and Bauckham read this as including Jesus in the identity of the one God, not adding a second god. Some scholars see it as Wisdom language for Jesus as the pattern of creation, not as a claim of pre-existence. Some Jewish readers see here the point at which Christianity parted from Judaism; Some scholars argue that some Jews of the time already thought of God as having a second divine figure. See the card.
r: Deuteronomy 6:4; 1 Corinthians 8:4; Colossians 1:16; John 1:3; Philippians 2:11; Romans 10:9

p: 'Through whom are all things' gives Jesus a part in the creation, a claim made also in John and Colossians.
b: Here Paul says all things are "through" Jesus, as John 1:3 says of the Word and Colossians 1:16 says of the Son. In Jewish writings, God made the world by his Wisdom (Proverbs 8:22-31; Wisdom of Solomon 9:1-2). Paul gives that role to Christ. Readings differ on whether it means the pre-existent Son (the Nicene tradition) or Wisdom's pattern now seen in Jesus. The second half, "and we are through him," points to the new creation in which Christians now live.

p: Conscience here is the inner voice that judges one's own acts; 'weak' people feel eating idol food as a betrayal.
b: Syneidēsis means "knowing with oneself": the inner judge of one's own actions. Paul uses it eight times in 8:7-12 and chapter 10, more than anywhere else. The "weak" are not weak in faith in general; they are believers whose old ties to idol worship make eating the meat feel like joining the worship. Likely people: former pagans for whom the meat still meant the god (as 8:7 says, "used to idols until now"). Others suggest Jewish believers who kept the food laws. Paul does not say that the weak are right, only that they must not be pushed. Compare Romans 14, where weak and strong disagree over food and days.

a: Food will not bring us before God.
p: Paul and Jesus both say that what a person eats does not decide their standing with God.
b: The verb paristēmi means "present, bring before," as in presenting an offering. Paul's statement agrees with Mark 7:15-19, where Mark adds that Jesus declared all foods clean, with Romans 14:17, where the kingdom of God is not a matter of food and drink, and with Colossians 2:16-23. It also rests on Romans 14:14, where Paul says nothing is unclean in itself. He does not say that food has no effect on others. This is why he can accept eating in principle (10:25-27) and yet refuse to do it in front of a weaker believer (8:13).

a: something for the weak to trip over
p: A stumbling block is anything in the path that trips a believer; Paul applies it to the strong's right to eat.
b: Proskomma is something you hit your foot on. The same idea is in the law against putting an obstacle in front of a blind person (Leviticus 19:14, where the Greek word is skandalon), and proskomma itself is the word of the stone of stumbling in the Greek of Isaiah 8:14. Paul uses the idea in Romans 14:13, where he tells believers not to put an obstacle in a brother's way, and sets a standard that love, not personal right, rules practice. "Right" is exousia, the "authority" of 6:12; 7:4; 9:4-6, 12, 18. The strong have the right, and Paul asks them to give it up.

a: sitting at a meal in an idol's temple
p: Paul pictures a believer eating in a pagan temple dining room, where a weaker believer might see him.
b: The word eidōleion is rare. It appears here and in some Greek Old Testament books (for example 1 Maccabees 10:83). The "knowing" Corinthian is at a banquet, reclining at table in the temple. Such meals were social: a wedding, a guild dinner, a family birthday, a business friend's gift. To refuse was to risk offense and loss of trade. Paul does not forbid the meal here on its own grounds. He deals first with its effect on the weak, then, in 10:14-22, he deals with the meal itself and says to "flee idolatry." So 8:10 is not the whole of his view. The words "built up" are irony: the weak person is encouraged to do something against his conscience.

a: is being destroyed by your knowledge
p: Paul says Christ died for the brother who is 'destroyed'; churches differ on whether a believer can be lost.
b: "Destroyed" (apollymi) is the word for perishing. It sits with "a brother for whom Christ died," so Paul speaks of someone Christ died for. Wesleyan and Catholic readers take it as proof that a believer can fall from grace. Reformed readers answer that Paul warns about what the act would cause, or about what appears to be a true believer, while God keeps his own (Romans 8:30). Others note that Paul uses it as a rhetorical warning, to show how serious a lack of love is. See the card on perseverance for each side. The later text has "will be destroyed" (see the variant).

a: I will never eat meat at all
p: Paul puts himself forward as an example, and chapter 9 develops it with his giving up of his rights.
b: Paul does not ask the strong to do something he will not do. He would give up all meat, not only idol meat, because he might not know where it came from. The same words appear in Romans 14:21: "It is good not to eat meat or drink wine, or do anything else that makes your brother stumble." The principle is that rights are for the sake of others. Paul says he has "the right" to many things (9:4-6) and uses none of them. Chapter 9 gives his examples, and chapter 10 returns to the issue with exact rules.
